American Politics. The systems, actors, and ideological struggles that shape governance in the United States—a republic founded on principles of democracy, constitutional checks and balances, and popular sovereignty, yet perpetually contested by regional factions, class interests, and competing visions of national purpose.

From the founding conflicts between Federalists and Anti-Federalists through Jacksonian democracy, the Civil War, Gilded Age politics, and twentieth-century partisan realignments, American political history reveals how constitutional structures interact with mass mobilization, economic change, and social movements to shape the nation's direction.

The American two-party system—Democrats and Republicans—is not mandated by the Constitution but evolved from competing coalitions. These rivals have existed since the early republic. The presidency, Congress, and courts operate under separation of powers. No single branch can dominate, creating perpetual friction and negotiation.

Suffrage expansion fundamentally transformed electoral politics and party coalitions. The right to vote expanded from property-owning white men to women, African Americans, and eighteen-year-olds. The Civil War realigned American politics dramatically. Reconstruction briefly empowered African American voters in the South, then Jim Crow disenfranchised them for a century.

Political parties are mass organizations competing for votes. They coalesce around regional interests—South versus North, rural versus urban—class, and ideology. Campaign finance and media—from newspapers to television to social media—shape electoral competition and who can be heard. Money in politics has grown exponentially. American exceptionalism—the idea that U.S. democracy is unique and superior—has shaped domestic politics and foreign policy. This mythology has justified both democratic idealism and imperial ambitions, making it a powerful and contested force in American political discourse.
